title: Harry Brook All But Closes the Door on IPL Return, Chooses England Over Franchise Cricket
excerpt: England's white-ball captain says he has no plans to play franchise cricket beyond The Hundred, signaling the IPL may have permanently lost one of cricket's most destructive batters.
body:
• Harry Brook has said he sees no way to fit the IPL into his schedule, preferring to use the three-month window for rest and fitness ahead of England duties.
  • The BCCI banned Brook until 2028 after he withdrew from two consecutive IPL seasons with Delhi Capitals, making him the first overseas player sanctioned under a new "commitment clause."
  • Brook captains England in both white-ball formats and is the leading candidate to succeed Ben Stokes as Test captain, making his schedule among the most demanding in world cricket.
  • IPL franchises may face a broader challenge retaining top English players as the ECB prioritizes international commitments over franchise leagues.

Brook Makes His Position Clear

Speaking ahead of England's T20I series against India in July, England captain Harry Brook delivered what may be his most definitive statement yet on franchise cricket. The 27-year-old said he has no plans to play in any franchise league outside The Hundred, the ECB's domestic competition, effectively ruling out an IPL return even when his ban expires.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=yWnyNgxm-po

"I think going to the IPL is a great experience. I really enjoyed my time when I went. But I don't see the world in how I can play it at the minute. Those three months are a perfect time for me to have a break and work hard on my fitness."

— Harry Brook, England Captain

Brook's comments carry weight because they come from a position of strength. He led England to a dominant T20I series victory over India, scoring an unbeaten 79 off 35 balls in the fourth match at Bristol to clinch the series. His form has been exceptional across formats, making his absence from the IPL all the more conspicuous.

The Ban That Started It All

Brook's complicated relationship with the IPL began with Sunrisers Hyderabad, who paid ₹13.25 crore for him ahead of IPL 2023 — his only season in the tournament. Delhi Capitals bought him for ₹4 crore ahead of IPL 2024, but he withdrew citing the death of his grandmother. When Delhi retained him at ₹6.25 crore for 2025, he pulled out again to focus on England commitments.

The repeated withdrawals triggered the BCCI's new commitment clause, introduced specifically to address the frustration of franchises left scrambling for replacements after auction. Brook became the first overseas player sanctioned under the rule, earning a ban through 2027, with eligibility returning only at the 2028 mega auction.

But his latest comments suggest the ban is moot. Even without it, Brook appears to have no interest in returning.

What It Means for IPL Franchises

Brook's absence deprives the IPL of one of the most destructive batters in world cricket. His ability to score at strike rates above 150 while maintaining consistency made him a franchise dream. The ₹13.25 crore that SRH spent in 2023 reflected his premium value.

The broader concern for IPL franchises is whether Brook represents a trend among top English cricketers. The ECB has increasingly emphasized workload management for multi-format players, and Brook's position as captain in two formats makes the scheduling conflict acute. With England's Test, ODI, and T20I commitments stretching year-round, the IPL's two-and-a-half-month window directly competes with preparation and recovery time.

The situation mirrors, in reverse, India's own reluctance to release top players for overseas franchise leagues. The IPL's dominance in the cricket economy has historically given it first claim on the world's best talent, but players like Brook — who prioritize national duty over the financial rewards of franchise cricket — represent a countertrend.

The Road Ahead

Brook is widely expected to be named England's Test captain following Ben Stokes's retirement from international cricket. If that appointment comes, he would lead England across all three formats — an all-consuming role that would make any franchise commitment virtually impossible.

For now, Brook's message to the IPL is unambiguous: England comes first, fitness comes second, and franchise cricket is not on the agenda. Whether that calculus changes as he ages and the financial incentives grow remains to be seen, but the IPL's loss is England cricket's gain.
